I read both files in full: `layers/http/__init__.py` (1211 lines) and `http.py` (1296 lines). Here's the map.

---

## Part 1: `mitmproxy/proxy/layers/http/__init__.py`

### The four layers in this file

| Class | Role |
|---|---|
| **`HttpLayer`** (`:921`) | Router. Owns every HTTP connection and stream for one client connection. |
| **`HttpStream`** (`:159`) | One request/response exchange. This is where the `HTTPFlow` is created and the addon hooks fire. |
| **`HttpClient`** (`:1191`) | Opens a server connection, then turns into `Http1Client`, `Http2Client` or `Http3Client` depending on ALPN. |
| `Http{1,2,3}{Server,Client}` | Wire codecs (imported from `_http1/2/3`, which I didn't read). They turn bytes into `HttpEvent`s and back. |

The `HttpLayer` docstring describes the pipeline:

```
ConnectionEvent (bytes) → HttpEvent (RequestHeaders…) → HttpCommand (SendHttp…) → ConnectionCommand (bytes out)
```

### How `HttpLayer` routes (`_handle_event` `:951`, `event_to_child` `:1021`)

Its state is four dicts:
- `connections: Connection → layer`: which codec or stack handles each socket.
- `streams: stream_id → HttpStream`
- `command_sources: Command → child`: records which child sent each blocking command (and each `RequestWakeup`), so the matching `CommandCompleted` goes back to that child.
- `waiting_for_establishment: Connection → [GetHttpConnection]`: streams waiting for a connection that is still opening.

What happens to each incoming event:
- **`Start`**: creates `Http3Server`, `Http2Server` or `Http1Server` based on the client's ALPN (`setdefault`, because client playback may have set one already). In upstream mode it also sets `server.via`.
- **`CommandCompleted`**: pops `command_sources` and sends the event to the child that issued the command.
- **`MessageInjected`**: skips the codecs and goes straight to the stream. It looks the stream up through `server_conn`, and falls back to `client_conn` for tunneled connections (HTTP/1 only; the comment says so).
- **`ConnectionEvent`**: goes to `connections[event.connection]`. One special case: if the server sends data before mitmproxy has used that connection (for example an h2 SETTINGS frame), a client codec is created on the spot.

What happens to each command a child yields (`event_to_child`):
- `ReceiveHttp(RequestHeaders)` → `make_stream()` creates a new `HttpStream`, then the event is forwarded to it. Events for streams that no longer exist are dropped (#5343).
- `SendHttp(event, conn)` → passed to the codec for `conn`.
- `DropStream` → removes the stream.
- `GetHttpConnection` → `get_connection()`
- `RegisterHttpConnection` → `register_connection()`
- `OpenConnection` → records the child as owner of that connection, then passes the command up.
- Anything else is passed up unchanged.

### Getting a server connection (`get_connection` `:1067`)

1. **Reuse** a connection that matches on address, tls, via and transport. If it's still opening, queue behind it. If it errored, return the error. If it's connected, use it, except for h2 client to non-h2 server.
2. Otherwise, use `context.server` if it matches and nothing has claimed it yet.
3. Otherwise **build a stack**: `[HttpUpstreamProxy if via] / [ServerTLSLayer or ServerQuicLayer if tls] / HttpClient`.
   - In upstream mode mitmproxy sends `CONNECT` to the upstream proxy, except for plaintext requests, which go as absolute-form.
   - SNI in transparent mode, in order of preference: the existing server SNI (reverse mode may set it), then the client's SNI, then the address.
4. `HttpClient` opens the connection and yields `RegisterHttpConnection`. `register_connection` then answers every waiting `GetHttpConnection`.
   - **H2→H1 edge case:** if the client speaks h2 and the server speaks HTTP/1, only the first waiter gets the connection. Every other waiter gets a fresh connection, because a read-until-EOF response can't share one.

### `HttpStream`: two state machines

The stream keeps `client_state` (the request side) and `server_state` (the response side) separately. Protocol errors go to `handle_protocol_error`. Request events go to `client_state`, everything else to `server_state`.

**Normal buffered flow, in order:**

```
RequestHeaders ─► state_wait_for_request_headers
   • create HTTPFlow(client, server) or reuse event.replay_flow; flow.live = True
   • check_invalid (scheme, CONNECT in transparent mode, header smuggling checks)
   • CONNECT? → handle_connect (see below)
   • fill in host/port/scheme: transparent → from server address; otherwise from Host header
   • regular mode + HTTP/1 → authority="" (forces origin-form, #1759)
   • reverse mode → rewrite Host header unless keep_host_header
   • check_body_size (early, uses Content-Length)
   ★ requestheaders hook  → check_killed
   • Expect: 100-continue → mitmproxy sends the 100 itself and removes the header
   • request.stream? → start_request_stream  :  client_state = consume_request_body
   • server_state = wait_for_response_headers

RequestData/Trailers/EOM ─► state_consume_request_body
   • buffer (check_body_size runs on each chunk, so streaming can switch on mid-body)
   ★ request hook → check_killed
   • if an addon set flow.response: fake the responseheaders hook, then send_response()
   • else make_server_connection → send Headers [+Data] [+Trailers] + EOM to server

ResponseHeaders ─► state_wait_for_response_headers
   • check_body_size, check_invalid (closes the server connection if invalid)
   ★ responseheaders hook → check_killed
   • response.stream? → start_response_stream  :  consume_response_body

ResponseData/Trailers/EOM ─► state_consume_response_body → send_response()
   • detect WebSocket upgrade (101 + upgrade: websocket + version + option), set flow.websocket BEFORE the hook
   ★ response hook → server_state = done → check_killed
   • send Headers/Data/Trailers to client
   • if client side is also done → flow_done()

flow_done()
   • live = False (unless websocket)
   • 101 → child layer = WebsocketLayer, or TCPLayer if rawtcp, else warn and close; switch to passthrough
   • otherwise DropStream
   • ResponseEndOfMessage is sent last, so the child layer is ready for any data that follows
```

**Streaming** (`state_stream_request_body` / `state_stream_response_body`): each chunk is forwarded as it arrives. If `stream` is a callable, it rewrites each chunk and gets a final call with `b""` at EOM to flush. Bodies are only kept if `store_streamed_bodies` is on. For streamed requests, the `request` hook fires at EOM, after the body has already gone out. Trailers are held back until after the hook.

**`check_body_size`** (`:568`): it finds the expected size from Content-Length, or from the bytes buffered so far, then:
- **Above `body_size_limit`**: it fires the `*headers` hook if that hasn't fired yet (so addons see the flow), then the error hook, and returns `ResponseProtocolError` to the client.
- **Above `stream_large_bodies`**: it switches to streaming. If bytes are already buffered, it replays them by calling `handle_event(RequestData(...))` on itself.

**`check_killed`** (`:696`): a flow counts as killed in two cases. Either an addon set `flow.error` to `KILLED_MESSAGE`, or a `RequestProtocolError` is waiting in `_paused_event_queue` (the client hung up while a hook was running).

**`handle_protocol_error`** (`:723`):
- If the client errors after the request is already going upstream, the error is forwarded to the server.
- The error hook fires only if no `response` hook has run, so a flow never gets both.
- It always ends with `DropStream`.

**CONNECT** (`handle_connect` `:773`):
- ★ `http_connect` hook → set `server.address`.
- Regular mode: with `connection_strategy == "eager"` the connection is opened immediately. If that fails, mitmproxy makes a 502 response; otherwise the child is `NextLayer`.
- Upstream mode: the child is `HttpUpstreamProxy`.
- `handle_connect_finish`: if no response exists yet, it makes a `200 Connection established` with **empty headers** (for Android emulator compatibility).
  - 2xx → ★ `http_connected`, then passthrough.
  - Anything else → ★ `http_connect_error`.

**`passthrough`** (`:847`): after CONNECT or a 101, the stream wraps an ordinary byte-level child layer and converts between the two worlds:
- `RequestData` ↔ `DataReceived(client)`, `ResponseData` ↔ `DataReceived(server)`
- EOM → `ConnectionClosed`
- Server-bound `SendData`/`CloseConnection` are wrapped as HTTP only after a 101. After CONNECT there's no HTTP server connection, so they pass through as plain commands.
- `CloseTcpConnection` (a half-close) becomes a full close.

### Hook order, summarized
- Plain request: `requestheaders` → `request` → `responseheaders` → `response`, or `error` at any point.
- CONNECT: `http_connect` → `http_connected` or `http_connect_error`.

---

## Part 2: `mitmproxy/http.py`: what flows carry

### The storage split
Every message has a `.data` dataclass that stores **raw bytes**. The `Message`/`Request`/`Response` classes put a `str` API on top of it.
- `MessageData`: `http_version, headers, content, trailers, timestamp_start, timestamp_end`. Types are checked in `__post_init__` when `__debug__` is on. It handles serialization via `get_state`/`set_state`.
- `RequestData` adds `host (str), port (int), method, scheme, authority, path` (all bytes).
- `ResponseData` adds `status_code, reason`.

The proxy layer writes to `request.data.host`/`.port` directly to **skip** the property setters, because `Request.host = …` also rewrites the Host header and authority (`_update_host_and_authority` `:767`).

### `Headers` (`:49`)
- A case-insensitive `MultiDict` stored as `(bytes, bytes)` field tuples, read and written as `str` (utf-8 with surrogateescape).
- Repeated headers are folded with `", "` on read. Setting a key replaces all its values.
- Use `get_all`/`set_all` for Cookie and Set-Cookie.
- In the constructor, `content_type=` becomes `content-type`.

### `Message` (`:233`)
- `stream`: `False`, `True`, or a chunk-transforming callable. It only takes effect if set in a `*headers` hook.
- Three views of the body:
  - `raw_content`: the bytes as sent, possibly compressed. It's `None` when the body was streamed and not stored.
  - `content`: decoded per `Content-Encoding`.
  - `text`: also decoded per the charset.
- Setting `content` re-encodes it and updates `content-length`, unless `transfer-encoding` is present. An invalid content-encoding gets removed.
- Also: `decode()`/`encode()`, `json()`, `is_http10/11/2/3`, `trailers`, timestamps.

### `Request` (`:516`)
- `host_header`: maps to the `Host` header on HTTP/1 and to `:authority` on h2/h3.
- `url` reads and writes scheme, host, port and path together. `pretty_host`/`pretty_url` prefer the Host header, which is useful in transparent mode but can be spoofed.
- `first_line_format`: `authority` (CONNECT), `absolute`, or `relative`.
- Live `MultiDictView`s that write back to path, headers or body: `query`, `cookies`, `urlencoded_form`, `multipart_form`.
- Helpers: `make()`, `anticache()`, `anticomp()`, `constrain_encoding()`.

### `Response` (`:1013`)
- `status_code`; `reason` (decoded as Latin-1).
- `cookies` maps name → `(value, attrs)`. Changing `attrs` in place does nothing; you have to reassign the tuple.
- `refresh()` shifts dates and cookie expiry for replay. `make()` builds a response.

### `HTTPFlow` (`:1210`)
- `request`, `response | None`, `error | None` (a flow can have both a response and an error), `websocket | None`.
- The rest comes from `flow.Flow`: `client_conn`, `server_conn`, `live`, and more. I didn't read `flow.py`.
- `timestamp_start` is an alias for the request's. `copy()` deep-copies the request and response. `mode` is deprecated.

---

### Notes from the read
- In `state_consume_request_body`, a request hook that sets `flow.response` skips the server entirely, and mitmproxy fakes the `responseheaders` hook (`:380`). That's how addons serve local responses.
- `check_body_size` calls `self.handle_event(...)` on its own stream (`:641`, `:649`), so it runs re-entrantly while the outer handler is still going.
- Two small typing nits: `passthrough`'s `@expect(..., events.Event)` accepts every event, so the filter does nothing. `state_stream_request_body`'s type hint leaves out `RequestTrailers`, which it does handle.

The pieces I didn't read are the wire codecs (`_http1.py`, `_http2.py`, `_http3.py`), the event and hook definitions (`_events.py`, `_hooks.py`) and `flow.py`. They're the natural next files if you want to see how bytes become `RequestHeaders`.

I've read all three files in full. Here's how TLS and HTTP/2 sit underneath the HTTP layer you already saw.

## `proxy/layers/tls.py` — the TLS tunnel

### `TLSLayer` (base, `:242`)
It's a `tunnel.TunnelLayer`, so it wraps a connection and converts ciphertext ↔ plaintext while a child layer runs on the decrypted stream. It owns an `OpenSSL.SSL.Connection` (`self.tls`) driven through a memory BIO:

- **`start_tls` (`:268`)** builds a `TlsData`, fires `TlsStartClientHook` or `TlsStartServerHook` depending on which side `self.conn` is, and expects the hook to have populated `tls_start.ssl_conn`. No context → log + close. This is the seam the `tlsconfig` addon fills.
- **`receive_handshake_data` (`:294`)** feeds bytes into the BIO (`bio_write`), calls `do_handshake()`. `WantReadError` → flush whatever handshake bytes OpenSSL wants to send (`tls_interact`) and return "not done yet". On success it records peer certs, `alpn`, `cipher`, `tls_version` onto the `Connection`, fires `TlsEstablished{Client,Server}Hook`, then calls `receive_data(b"")` to drain any app data already buffered. The big `SSL.Error` ladder translates OpenSSL errors into human messages (cert verify failed, "remote server does not speak TLS", version mismatch).
- **`receive_data` / `send_data` (`:408`, `:452`)** are the steady-state pumps: `recv`/`sendall` on the TLS object, `bio_read`/`bio_write` against the socket, decrypted bytes go to the child via `DataReceived`, `ZeroReturnError` becomes `ConnectionClosed`.

### `ServerTLSLayer` (`:467`) and `ClientTLSLayer` (`:515`)
These are the two subclasses that encode mitmproxy's defining trick: **it must usually talk to the server before it can impersonate it to the client**, because the client's ALPN/SNI choice and the real cert should inform what mitmproxy presents.

- `ClientTLSLayer.receive_handshake_data` (`:562`) buffers bytes until it can parse a complete ClientHello (`parse_client_hello`), extracts SNI and ALPN offers onto `context.client`, and fires **`TlsClienthelloHook`**. If the hook sets `establish_server_tls_first`, it calls `start_server_tls` → `OpenConnection(context.server)` *before* doing its own `start_tls`. That's the ordering dependency.
- `ServerTLSLayer.start_handshake` (`:477`) is the mirror: if its immediate child is a `ClientTLSLayer`, it sets `wait_for_clienthello = True` and stays closed, so the client side can drive. When the client layer emits `OpenConnection`, the server layer swallows it (`:496`) and proceeds. If there's no client TLS below it (e.g. eager connection, plain server), it handshakes immediately.
- `ClientTLSLayer` also handles **ignore_connection** (`:586`): if the clienthello hook decides not to intercept, it swaps in fake connection objects and a passthrough `TCPLayer`/`UDPLayer` so raw bytes flow untouched. And TLS-over-TLS (`:537`) resets the outer client attributes so only the inner session is recorded.

This is where the `event.tls` branch in `HttpLayer.get_connection` (that you saw building `stack /= tls.ServerTLSLayer(context)`) actually lands.

## `addons/tlsconfig.py` — the addon that supplies SSL contexts

`TLSLayer` deliberately knows nothing about certificates. This addon implements the `tls_start_*` hooks and produces the `SSL.Connection` objects.

- **`tls_clienthello` (`:232`)** sets `establish_server_tls_first = server.tls and connection_strategy == "eager"` — i.e. only connect upstream first in eager mode. That's the policy behind the layer ordering above.
- **`tls_start_client` (`:238`)** is the "mitmproxy as a server" side. It calls `get_cert` to mint/fetch a leaf cert, builds a server-side `SSL.Context`, and crucially installs `alpn_select_callback`.
- **`tls_start_server` (`:302`)** is the "mitmproxy as a client" side. It sets SNI (client's SNI → address fallback), configures peer verification (`ssl_insecure` → VERIFY_NONE), enables hostname/IP validation on the X509 params, and sets the ALPN offers to forward upstream.
- **`get_cert` (`:634`)** decides the CN/SANs: it prefers the **upstream** cert's CN + altnames + organization (when `upstream_cert` is on and the server cert is known), plus the client SNI and the known server address. This is why an intercepted cert looks like the real site's cert.
- `quic_start_client`/`quic_start_server` (`:408`, `:449`) do the same job for QUIC/H3, kept deliberately in sync with the TLS versions.

### ALPN negotiation — how the HTTP version gets chosen
`alpn_select_callback` (`:108`) is the linchpin tying TLS to the HTTP layer. Reading `AppData`:
1. If the client's ALPN is pinned (`client_alpn` set), echo it or refuse.
2. Else prefer what the **server** negotiated (`server_alpn`) — mitmproxy mirrors the upstream protocol so the two legs match.
3. Else pick from `HTTP_ALPNS` (includes `h2`) if `http2` option is on, otherwise `HTTP1_ALPNS` only.

The negotiated protocol lands on `conn.alpn` during the handshake (`tls.py:380`). That is exactly the value `HttpLayer._handle_event` reads at `Start` to choose `Http2Server` vs `Http1Server`, and `HttpClient`/`get_connection` reads on the server side to choose `Http2Client` vs `Http1Client`. **ALPN is the handoff from the TLS layer to the HTTP codec selection you saw in part 1.** Note the deliberate forcing of `http/1.1` for secure web proxies (`:286`) because CONNECT-over-h2 isn't supported.

## `http/_http2.py` — the HTTP/2 codec

This is one of the `Http*Server`/`Http*Client` codecs that `HttpLayer` instantiates. It sits between raw `DataReceived`/`SendData` bytes and the `HttpEvent` stream (`RequestHeaders`, `RequestData`, …) that `HttpStream` consumes. It wraps the `h2` (hyper-h2) state machine via `BufferedH2Connection`.

### `Http2Connection` (base, `:65`)
Two translation directions:

- **HttpEvent → h2 (`_handle_event`, `:123`)**: `RequestData`/`ResponseData` → `send_data`, trailers → `send_trailers`, EOM → `end_stream`, and `Request/ResponseProtocolError` → either a synthesized error response (if we can still send headers) or `reset_stream` with an h2 error code mapped from mitmproxy's `ErrorCode` enum (the big `match` at `:163`). Every branch ends by flushing `data_to_send()` as `SendData`.
- **h2 events → HttpEvent (`handle_h2_event`, `:225`)**: `DataReceived` → `ReceiveHttp(ReceiveData(...))` plus flow-control acknowledgement; `TrailersReceived`, `StreamEnded` → EOM; `StreamReset` → a `ReceiveProtocolError`; `ConnectionTerminated`/`ProtocolError` tear down. Push promises are rejected (push is disabled). The `streams` dict tracks `EXPECTING_HEADERS` vs `HEADERS_RECEIVED` to catch protocol violations (data before headers).

`ReceiveProtocolError`/`ReceiveData`/`ReceiveTrailers`/`ReceiveEndOfMessage` are class attributes that the two subclasses point at the request or response variants — that's how one base class serves both directions.

### `Http2Server` (`:406`) vs `Http2Client` (`:474`)
- **Server** (binds `context.client`, `client_side=False`): on `RequestReceived` it calls `parse_h2_request_headers` to split pseudo-headers (`:method`, `:scheme`, `:path`, `:authority`) from real headers, builds an `http.Request` with `http_version=b"HTTP/2.0"`, and emits `RequestHeaders`. Its `ReceiveData` etc. are the *request* types. This feeds the `HttpStream` state machine you mapped in part 1.
- **Client** (binds `context.server`, `client_side=True`): the inverse — emits `ResponseHeaders` from `ResponseReceived`. It disables push, and adds two HTTP/2-specific concerns:
  - **Stream-ID remapping (`_handle_event`, `:505`)**: outside stream ids (assigned by the client, possibly reordered) are mapped to freshly allocated upstream ids via `our_stream_id`/`their_stream_id`, because h2 forbids opening a lower id than a previous one. Incoming `ReceiveHttp` events get mapped back.
  - **Concurrency queue**: if `open_outbound_streams` hits `MAX_CONCURRENT_STREAMS` (with a provisional limit of 10 before the server's first SETTINGS), new streams are parked in `stream_queue` and replayed FIFO when capacity frees up.
  - **Ping keepalive (`_handle_event2`, `:539`)**: uses `RequestWakeup`/`Wakeup` (the blocking-command mechanism `HttpLayer` routes back via `command_sources`) to send periodic PING frames per `http2_ping_keepalive`.

### Header normalization
`format_h2_request_headers`/`format_h2_response_headers` (`:364`, `:390`) build the pseudo-header block and, when the message originated as HTTP/1 (`normalize_h1_headers`), lowercase header names so they're valid h2. On HTTP/1 requests without `:authority`, the `Host` header is promoted to `:authority`. `parse_h2_*` do the reverse split. This is the concrete mechanism behind mitmproxy's protocol translation — an h2 client talking to an h1 server works because `HttpStream` sees uniform `http.Request`/`http.Response` objects regardless of wire version.

## How it all stacks up

For an intercepted HTTPS/h2 connection, the layer stack from bytes upward is:

```
socket bytes
  └─ ClientTLSLayer      (parse ClientHello → TlsClienthelloHook → maybe open server first)
       │  ← tlsconfig.tls_start_client supplies the faked cert + alpn_select_callback
       │  ← ALPN negotiates "h2" onto context.client.alpn
       └─ HttpLayer(mode)
            ├─ Http2Server         (client-facing codec; DataReceived → RequestHeaders)
            ├─ HttpStream (per req) (HTTPFlow, hooks: requestheaders/request/response/...)
            └─ server stack built on demand in get_connection:
                 [HttpUpstreamProxy?] / ServerTLSLayer / HttpClient
                      │  ← tlsconfig.tls_start_server sets SNI + verify + ALPN offers
                      │  ← server ALPN "h2" → Http2Client chosen
                      └─ Http2Client  (server-facing codec; ResponseReceived → ResponseHeaders)
```

The three interlocking seams worth remembering:
1. **The `tls_start_*` hooks** are how the generic `TLSLayer` gets its cert/context from the `tlsconfig` addon — the layer does crypto, the addon does policy.
2. **ALPN** (chosen in `alpn_select_callback`, stored on `conn.alpn`) is what decides HTTP/1 vs HTTP/2 vs HTTP/3 on each leg — read in exactly the spots you saw in `__init__.py`.
3. **`ReceiveHttp`/`SendHttp` of `HttpEvent`s** is the uniform interface: `Http2Server`/`Http2Client` translate h2 frames to/from the same `RequestHeaders`/`ResponseData`/… events that `HttpStream` processes identically regardless of protocol version, which is what makes cross-version proxying (h2↔h1) and the h2→h1 multiplexing edge case in `register_connection` possible.

A note on what I didn't read: `BufferedH2Connection`/`_http_h2.py` (the buffering wrapper over hyper-h2), `tunnel.py` (the `TunnelLayer` base), and `net/tls.py` (the `create_*_context` builders). Those are the next files if you want the mechanics below these.

I've read all four files. Here's how filtering reaches the view, and how the HAR addon writes its file.

## Part 1: A filter typed in the UI → applied to the view

### Step 1: parsing the string (`flowfilter.py`)
A filter is text like `~u example\.com & ~c 200`. The grammar is built once at import (`_make()`, `:737`) into the module-level `bnf` parser (`:784`), using pyparsing.

- Each filter class has a `code` and a matcher `__call__(self, f) -> bool`. They fall into three groups registered in `_make()`:
  - **unary** (`~q`, `~s`, `~e`, `~marked`, `~http`, `~all`, …) — no argument.
  - **rex** (`~u`, `~d`, `~h`, `~b`, `~m`, …) — take a regex argument.
  - **int** (`~c`) — take a number.
- Operators are wired via `pp.infix_notation` (`:772`): `!` (not), `&` (and), `|` (or), plus parens. A bare regex with no `~` prefix becomes `~u` (URL), handled by `FUrl.make` (`:510`, `:766`).
- `parse(s)` (`:797`) runs `bnf.parse_string(s, parse_all=True)[0]`, stamps `.pattern = s` on the result, and raises `ValueError` on bad syntax. The returned object is a composite of `FAnd`/`FOr`/`FNot`/leaf actions — each is callable, so the whole tree is **one callable** `flt(flow) -> bool`.

The leaf matchers read flow attributes directly: `FUrl` matches `f.request.pretty_url` (`:521`), `FCode` compares `f.response.status_code` (`:637`), `FBod` searches decoded content with `get_content(strict=False)`, etc. The `@only(...)` decorator (`:64`) short-circuits to `False` for flow types a matcher doesn't apply to, so an HTTP-only filter silently excludes TCP/DNS/UDP flows. Regexes are case-insensitive unless `MITMPROXY_CASE_SENSITIVE_FILTERS=1` (`:57`).

### Step 2: the View holds the active filter (`addons/view.py`)
The `View` addon keeps two collections:
- `self._store` — an `OrderedDict[id → flow]` of **every** flow (`:149`).
- `self._view` — a `SortedListWithKey` holding **only** the flows that currently pass the filter, in sort order (`:167`).

`self.filter` is the compiled `TFilter`, defaulting to `flowfilter.match_all` (`:152`, which is `parse("~all")`).

Two entry points set it:
- **Command** `view.filter.set` → `set_filter_cmd` (`:341`): this is what the console UI calls when you type a filter. It `flowfilter.parse()`s the string (re-raising `ValueError` as `CommandError` so the UI shows the message) and calls `set_filter`.
- **Option** `view_filter` → `configure` (`:563`): the same thing driven from the `--view-filter` option / options editor, raising `OptionsError` instead.

Both land in `set_filter` (`:354`):
```python
self.filter = flt or flowfilter.match_all
self._refilter()
```

### Step 3: `_refilter` rebuilds the view (`:250`)
```python
self._view.clear()
for i in self._store.values():
    if self.show_marked and not i.marked:
        continue
    if self.filter(i):          # ← the compiled filter callable
        self._base_add(i)
self.sig_view_refresh.send()
```
It walks the full store, drops anything not matching (and, if marked-only mode is on, anything unmarked), re-adds survivors to the sorted view, and fires `sig_view_refresh`. The UI is subscribed to that signal and redraws the flow list. `Focus._sig_view_refresh` (`:710`) also listens, so the selected row snaps to the nearest still-visible flow.

### Step 4: the filter also gates live updates
The filter isn't only applied on a full refilter — it's consulted every time a flow changes, so the view stays consistent as traffic arrives:
- **`add`** (`:511`, called from `requestheaders`/`tcp_start`/`dns_request` hooks): a new flow enters `_store` always, but only enters `_view` if `self.filter(f)` passes.
- **`update`** (`:634`, called from `response`/`error`/`intercept`/… hooks): when a flow mutates, it re-tests the filter. This is the important case — a flow that didn't match before (e.g. `~c 200` before the response arrived) gets **added** when it starts matching, and one that stops matching gets **removed** (`:653`). If it still matches and was already shown, `order_key.refresh(f)` re-sorts it (because a key like size changes over the flow's life, `:57`).

So the end-to-end path is: **UI text → `view.filter.set` command → `flowfilter.parse` → `set_filter` stores the callable → `_refilter` rebuilds `_view` → `sig_view_refresh` → UI redraws**, and thereafter every `add`/`update` re-applies the same callable per-flow.

One thing worth noting for where you'll be working: the filter is a plain Python predicate over flow attributes. `_refilter` is O(store size) and re-runs on every filter change; per-flow `update` is O(1) filter calls. There's no index — large stores re-scan linearly.

## Part 2: How the HAR export addon writes its file (`addons/savehar.py`)

### Two ways it runs
1. **On-demand command** `save.har` → `export_har` (`:35`): the UI/command passes a list of flows and a path.
2. **Automatic on exit**: the `hardump` option (`:78`). While running, the `response`/`error`/`websocket_end` hooks (`:104`–`:114`) call `_save_flow`, which appends matching flows to `self.flows` (only when `hardump` is set, `:117`). At shutdown, `done` (`:122`) dumps them — to stdout if `hardump == "-"`, else to the file via `export_har`.

Note the filter reuse: `self.filt` comes from the **`save_stream_filter`** option, parsed with the same `flowfilter.parse` (`:94`). So the save path uses the exact filtering machinery from Part 1, just a different option feeding it. WebSocket flows are deliberately held until `websocket_end` rather than saved at `response` (`:106`), so their messages are complete.

### Building the HAR structure (`make_har`, `:49`)
Produces the standard HAR 1.2 envelope: `{"log": {version, creator (mitmproxy + version), pages: [], entries: [...]}}`. It iterates the flows, converting each `HTTPFlow` via `flow_entry`; non-HTTP flows are counted and skipped with an info log (`:62`).

### Per-flow entry (`flow_entry`, `:130`)
This maps one `HTTPFlow` onto one HAR entry:
- **Timings** (`:133`–`:178`): `connect`/`ssl` are computed from the server connection's `timestamp_tcp_setup`/`timestamp_tls_setup`/`timestamp_start`, in milliseconds. The `servers_seen` set (threaded through from `make_har`, `:54`) ensures connection-setup time is only attributed to the **first** flow on a given `server_conn`; reused connections get `-1`. `send`/`wait`/`receive` come from request/response timestamp deltas. `entry["time"]` sums the non-negative timings (`:240`).
- **Response body** (`:180`): tries decoded `content`, falling back to `raw_content` on a decode `ValueError`. It records raw vs decoded size and the difference as `compression`. If the body `is_mostly_bin`, it's base64-encoded with `"encoding": "base64"`; otherwise stored as text (`:205`). A missing response yields a zeroed stub carrying `_error` from `flow.error` (`:214`).
- **Request** (`:236`): method, URL (`pretty_url`; CONNECT gets an `https://…/` form, `:231`), version, cookies/headers/query via `format_multidict`, and body size. For POST/PUT/PATCH it adds `postData` with the urlencoded form params (`:258`).
- **Extras**: `serverIPAddress` from the server peername (`:266`); for WebSocket flows, `_webSocketMessages` with each message as send/receive + base64 for binary (`:269`).
- Cookies: request cookies via `format_multidict`; response cookies via `format_response_cookies` (`:288`), which expands name/value/path/domain/httpOnly/secure/sameSite (expiry is explicitly punted, `:301`).

### Writing bytes (`export_har`, `:35`)
```python
har = json.dumps(self.make_har(flows), indent=4).encode()
if path.endswith(".zhar"):
    har = zlib.compress(har, 9)
with open(path, "wb") as f:
    f.write(har)
logging.log(ALERT, f"HAR file saved ({human.pretty_size(len(har))} bytes).")
```
So: serialize to pretty JSON bytes, optionally zlib-compress for a `.zhar` extension, write binary, and log an ALERT-level confirmation. (Minor: the logged size is the compressed length for `.zhar`, and the message says "bytes" even though `pretty_size` renders units like "1.2kb".)

## How these two files connect
The common thread is `flowfilter`: the **same** `parse()`/`TFilter` callable is the filtering primitive for both the live `View` (via `view_filter`) and the HAR save path (via `save_stream_filter`). The `View` keeps a store + a filtered sorted projection and pushes signals to the UI; `SaveHar` keeps its own flat `self.flows` list, filtered the same way, and serializes to HAR/zHAR on command or at exit. And both lean on the `Flow`/`HTTPFlow` attributes from `flow.py` — `error`, `marked`, `is_replay`, `live`, `server_conn` timestamps — that the matchers and the HAR timing/metadata fields read directly.

Files I didn't open but that border this: `io.FlowReader` (used by `view.flows.load`, `:501`), `coretypes/multidict` (the `items(multi=True)` the HAR formatter relies on), and `utils/signals` (the `SyncSignal` wiring the UI subscribes to).

## Run result

I ran `.venv/bin/python -m pytest test/mitmproxy -v`. pytest also picked up the default `addopts = "--capture=no --color=yes"` and asyncio settings from `pyproject.toml`, and I didn't change them.

**2016 passed, 5 skipped, 0 failed, in 12.95s.** The output was too long to show inline, so I saved it:
- `/tmp/mitm_pytest.log` has every test name, with color codes
- `/tmp/mitm_pytest.clean.log` is the same output with the colors stripped, easier to grep

The 5 skips are all environment-related:
- `addons/test_proxyserver.py::test_regular_http3`: HTTP/3 in regular mode isn't fully supported yet, so it's marked skip.
- `proxy/test_mode_servers.py::test_wireguard` and `test_wireguard_dual_stack[127.0.0.1 / ::1]`: the WireGuard test client doesn't support this machine's architecture.
- `proxy/test_mode_servers.py::test_tun_mode`: Linux-only.

The 6 warnings come from deprecations in dependencies (`pyasn1`, and `urwid`'s `get_item_size` called from the console UI). None of them come from mitmproxy's own code.

## How the tests are organised

The `test/mitmproxy` tree follows the `mitmproxy/` package layout: `mitmproxy/X/y.py` is tested in `test/mitmproxy/X/test_y.py`.

| Directory | Tests | What it covers |
|---|---|---|
| `addons/` | 540 | one file per addon: `test_view.py`, `test_savehar.py`, `test_tlsconfig.py`, … |
| top level | 424 | the core modules: `test_flowfilter.py`, `test_flow.py`, `test_http.py`, `test_tls.py`, `test_command.py`, … |
| `proxy/layers/` (+ `http/`, `quic/`) | 392 | the sans-IO layer state machines |
| `proxy/` | 76 | server, mode specs, mode servers, tunnel |
| `net/`, `net/http/`, `net/dns/` | 173 | wire parsing and encoding |
| `contentviews/` | 118 | body pretty-printers, with sample data in `test_*_data/` |
| `tools/console`, `tools/web` | 125 | the urwid console UI and the web UI |
| `coretypes/`, `io/`, `utils/`, `script/`, `platform/` | the rest | helpers and flow-file I/O |

Shared setup:
- `test/conftest.py` holds the platform skip markers (`skip_windows`, `skip_not_linux`, `skip_no_ipv6`), an eager-task asyncio event-loop policy, the `tdata` fixture (resolves paths under `test/mitmproxy/data/`), and a log-capture helper for async tests.
- `test/mitmproxy/data/` holds the fixture files: certificates, a confdir, saved flows, HAR files including corrupted ones, and addon scripts.
- Async tests need no decorator because `asyncio_mode = "auto"` is set.

## Where filters are covered

**`test/mitmproxy/test_flowfilter.py`** is the main filter suite:
- `TestParsing` covers the grammar: parse errors, naked-URL shorthand, quoting, nesting, `!` / `&` / `|`, non-ASCII input, and a parametrized check of each filter's `__str__` output.
- `TestMatchingHTTPFlow`, `TestMatchingDNSFlow`, `TestMatchingTCPFlow`, `TestMatchingUDPFlow` and `TestMatchingWebSocketFlow` run every operator against each flow type. They include the negative cases where `@only(...)` makes a filter return False for a flow type it doesn't apply to, for example `~c` on a TCP flow. `test_case_sensitive` checks the `MITMPROXY_CASE_SENSITIVE_FILTERS` environment variable.

Filters are also used in other tests:
- `addons/test_view.py`: `test_filter` covers filtering in the view (`set_filter`, refiltering, flows entering and leaving the view as they change), `test_resolve` covers `view.flows.resolve`, which accepts filter expressions, and `test_configure` covers an invalid `view_filter` raising `OptionsError`.
- `addons/test_savehar.py` and `addons/test_save.py` cover `save_stream_filter`.
- `test_flow.py`, `test_http.py`, `test_tcp.py`, `test_udp.py` and `test_dns.py` contain smaller filter-match checks.
- `tools/console/test_commander.py`, `test_statusbar.py` and `tools/web/test_static_viewer.py` cover the UI side.

## Where addons are covered

Each addon has its own `test/mitmproxy/addons/test_<addon>.py`. The two you'll work in:
- **`test_view.py`** tests ordering (`test_order_refresh`, `test_order_generators_*`, `test_reversed`), the store and view (`test_simple*`, `test_update`, `test_remove`, `test_duplicate`), the signals and focus logic (`test_signals`, `test_focus`, `test_focus_follow`), per-flow settings, and loading from a file.
- **`test_savehar.py`** tests cookie formatting, the per-connection timing logic (`test_seen_server_conn`, `test_tls_setup`, `test_timestamp_end`), binary/base64 bodies, `test_content_raises` (the `ValueError` fallback), a round trip against the HAR files in `data/`, and `TestHardumpOption` (the export-on-exit path).

To run just those while you work:

```
.venv/bin/python -m pytest test/mitmproxy/test_flowfilter.py test/mitmproxy/addons/test_view.py test/mitmproxy/addons/test_savehar.py -v
```

## What's been changing

The 40 commits run from January 2025 to October 2026. Nearly all are small bug fixes, and each touches only one or two files. Most of the work is in TLS, auth and the proxy edge. The files you'll be working in have barely changed.

**1. TLS certificate handling (`tlsconfig.py`) is the most active area.** It had three commits in the last two weeks: the `--emudhra` and `--emudhra-old` options, then blocking OCSP/CRL lookups for that certificate chain (#8500, #8503, #8516). Earlier work covered CRLs on the generated certificates (#7609) and moving off deprecated pyOpenSSL APIs (#7687, #7968). If you change `tls_start_*` or `get_cert`, expect conflicts with this ongoing work.

**2. `flowfilter.py` had one big change, and the rest is pyparsing maintenance.**
- **#8245 (July 2026) is the only substantial change, and it adds to `__str__`, which you saw tested in `TestParsing`.** Every filter class now has a human-readable `__str__` ("has error", "is marked", "is an HTTP Flow", …). `_Token`/`_Action` became abstract base classes with an abstract `__str__`, type hints were added throughout, and the pyparsing requirement went up to 3.3.2. So a new filter class must implement `__str__`, or it can't be instantiated.

**3. `view.py` and `savehar.py` are quiet.** In 22 months, `view.py` got one parameter correction (#8172) and one typo fix. `savehar.py` got one bug fix (#7666, "fix #7452"; the message doesn't say what changed). So there's no ongoing refactor to work around there. These files also have less recent attention, and their tests (`test_view.py`, `test_savehar.py`) are the main guide to how they're supposed to behave.

**4. Other recurring themes:**
- **Exports:** four fixes to curl/httpie/raw output correctness (Content-Length, escaping, surrogates).

- **Moving to the new contentview API** in `dumper.py` and `dns_resolver.py` (spring 2025).
- **Smaller additions and lint cleanups:** Edge support in the browser addon, and fixes for PEP 765 and pyupgrade.

Maximilian Hils, the maintainer, wrote about a third of these commits. Most of the rest come from one-off outside contributors, which suggests well-scoped bug-fix PRs are the usual way changes come in.

I reproduced the bug: every filter that takes no argument fails to parse when a `)` comes right after it. Adding a space before the `)` makes the same expression parse.

**Script:** `/tmp/flowfilter_repro/repro_paren.py`, run with `.venv/bin/python /tmp/flowfilter_repro/repro_paren.py`. It's outside the repo and I made no changes to the repo.

```
OK    '~s'
FAIL  '(~s)'                   Invalid filter expression: '(~s)'
OK    '(~s )'
FAIL  '!(~s)'                  Invalid filter expression: '!(~s)'
OK    '!(~s )'
FAIL  '~c 200 & !(~q)'         Invalid filter expression: '~c 200 & !(~q)'
OK    '~c 200 & !(~q )'
FAIL  '(~a)'                   Invalid filter expression: '(~a)'
FAIL  '(~websocket)'           Invalid filter expression: '(~websocket)'
OK    '(~websocket )'
OK    '(~c 200)'
OK    '(~d example.com)'
FAIL  '(~e)'  /  '(~marked)'  /  '(~http)'  /  '(~all)'   (same error)
```

Every case the user reported behaves as described. It's broader than their four examples: `~e`, `~marked`, `~http` and `~all` fail the same way, so it looks like it affects every no-argument filter in `filter_unary`. Filters that take an argument, like `(~c 200)` and `(~d example.com)`, parse fine.

**Likely cause:** `flowfilter.py:742` builds each no-argument filter as:

```python
f = pp.Literal(f"~{cls.code}") + pp.WordEnd()
```

By default, pyparsing's `WordEnd()` counts every printable character, including `)`, as part of a word. It only matches when the next character is whitespace or the end of the input. So in `~s)` it sees `)` as a continuation of the word and rejects it, the same way it correctly rejects `~sx`. I confirmed this directly with pyparsing 3.3.2: `~s)` fails with "Expected end of a word, found ')'".

The check is there for a reason. Without it, `~h` would match the start of `~hq` and `~s` the start of `~src`, which is why `_make` warns that order matters. Filters with an argument escape the bug because their argument comes after the `WordEnd()`, and nothing checks what follows it.

A likely fix is to give `WordEnd` an explicit set of word characters that leaves out `)`, for example `pp.WordEnd(pp.alphanums + "_-")`. Changing only the unary line would be enough for this bug. I haven't changed or tested anything, and `test_flowfilter.py` would need to keep passing. Want me to make the fix and add regression tests for these cases?

steps.text:
## Root cause

The check that marks where a no-argument filter's name ends treats `)` as part of the name. It's the `pp.WordEnd()` on `mitmproxy/flowfilter.py:742`, which runs with pyparsing's default set of word characters.

### The mitmproxy line

`mitmproxy/flowfilter.py:741-744`:
```python
    for cls in filter_unary:
        f = pp.Literal(f"~{cls.code}") + pp.WordEnd()
        f.set_parse_action(cls.make)
        parts.append(f)
```
A no-argument filter is the literal `~s` followed by `WordEnd()`, and nothing else. `WordEnd()` is called with no arguments, so it uses pyparsing's default.

### The pyparsing lines

`.venv/lib/python3.12/site-packages/pyparsing/core.py:4209-4234` (pyparsing 3.3.2):
```python
class WordEnd(PositionToken):
    """Matches if the current position is at the end of a :class:`Word`,
    and is not followed by any character in a given set of ``word_chars``
    (default= ``printables``). ...
    """
    def __init__(self, word_chars: str = printables, **kwargs) -> None:   # :4218
        ...
        self.wordChars = set(wordChars)                                    # :4223
        self.skipWhitespace = False                                        # :4224

    def parseImpl(self, instring, loc, do_actions=True):
        instrlen = len(instring)
        if instrlen > 0 and loc < instrlen:                                # :4229
            if (
                instring[loc] in self.wordChars                            # :4231
                or instring[loc - 1] not in self.wordChars
            ):
                raise ParseException(instring, loc, self.errmsg, self)     # :4234
        return loc, []
```
`printables` means every non-whitespace ASCII character, so `)` counts as a word character. `WordEnd` only matches when the next character is whitespace or the end of the input. It also sets `skipWhitespace = False`, so it looks at the character immediately after `~s`.

### How `(~s)` fails, step by step
1. `infix_notation` (`flowfilter.py:772`) consumes the `(` and tries to parse an `atom` at index 1.
2. The `atom` is a `MatchFirst(parts)` (`:770`) and tries the unary alternatives first. `Literal("~s")` matches indexes 1–2.
3. `WordEnd` runs at index 3. `instring[3]` is `)`, which is in `printables`, so the condition at `core.py:4231` is true and `:4234` raises.
4. Every other alternative fails too:
   - No rex or int filter has code `s`.
   - The bare-regex fallback can't start at a `~`, because `CharsNotIn("()~'\"" …)` on `:748` excludes it.
5. The atom fails, `parse_string(..., parse_all=True)` raises, and `parse()` turns that into `Invalid filter expression` on `flowfilter.py:809`.

The other forms in the report behave as follows:
- **`(~s )`** works: at index 3 the next character is a space, which isn't in `wordChars`, and the previous one is `s`, which is. `WordEnd` passes, `infix_notation` skips the space and matches the `)`.
- **Bare `~s`** works: `loc == instrlen`, so the guard at `core.py:4229` skips the check entirely.
- **`!(~s)` and `~c 200 & !(~q)`** fail exactly like `(~s)`. The `!` and `&` aren't the problem. It's always the `)` straight after the code.

### Why filters with arguments aren't affected
Lines 756 and 761 use the same `WordEnd()`:
```python
f = pp.Literal(f"~{cls.code}") + pp.WordEnd() + regex.copy()      # :756
f = pp.Literal(f"~{cls.code}") + pp.WordEnd() + pp.Word(pp.nums)  # :761
```
In those filters `WordEnd` runs between the code and its argument, where there's always a space (`~c 200`, `~d foo`), so it passes. Whatever follows the argument is never checked by `WordEnd`:
- The argument itself stops before the `)`. `CharsNotIn` on `:748` excludes `(` and `)`, and `Word(nums)` stops at non-digits.
- So `(~c 200)` and `(~d example.com)` parse.

A no-argument filter is the only kind where `WordEnd` is the last element, so it's the only kind that checks the character after the expression.

### Why `WordEnd` is there at all
It's needed, just with the wrong character set. It's what tells filter codes that share a prefix apart. I listed the prefix pairs from the code tables:

`a/all`, `s/src`, `h/hq/hs/http`, `d/dns/dst`, `t/tcp/tq/ts`, `m/marked/meta/marker`, `replay/replayq/replays`, `b/bq/bs`, `u/udp`, `c/comment`

Without it, `MatchFirst` could take `~a` out of `~all`, or `~h` out of `~hq`. `WordEnd` stops that, because the next character (`l`, `q`) is a word character. The bug is that the default `printables` set also contains the grammar's own operators and brackets.

The same problem shows up with `~s&~q` and `~s|~q`, which fail while `~s & ~q` works. I ran those too. So this isn't only about `)`. Any operator written directly after a no-argument filter breaks the parse.

### Not a recent regression
`git blame` attributes all three lines to `2239c49e18` (Maximilian Hils, 2019-11-15), and pyparsing's `WordEnd` has always defaulted to `printables`. So this has been the behaviour for years. It isn't fallout from this year's pyparsing renames (#8344) or the `__str__` rework (#8245).

### What a fix would change
The fix is to pass `WordEnd` an explicit set of characters that can appear inside a filter code, so operators and brackets count as boundaries. For example, `pp.WordEnd(pp.alphanums + "_")` on `:742` would do it, and could go on `:756`/`:761` as well for consistency. That still separates `~a` from `~all` and `~h` from `~hq`, and lets `)`, `&`, `|` and `!` end a code. I haven't made the change. To confirm it, `test_flowfilter.py` should keep passing and `/tmp/flowfilter_repro/repro_paren.py` should come back all-OK.

steps.text:
I reviewed the diff and widened the fix. A filter with no argument can now be followed directly by `&`, `|` and `!` as well as by brackets. Everything still passes:
- 124 tests in `test_flowfilter.py`
- the full suite: 2017 passed, 5 skipped (the same environment skips as before)
- ruff, mypy, and `git diff --check`

With only the fix reverted, the new tests fail in both `test_nesting_unary` and `test_binaryops`.

## What I changed and why

**1. The fix: the grammar's operators now end a filter name too** (`mitmproxy/flowfilter.py:741-746`)
```python
    # Filters without arguments may be directly followed by an operator or
    # bracket, e.g. "!(~s)" or "~s&~q", but "~sx" must still be rejected.
    unary_end = pp.WordEnd("".join(c for c in pp.printables if c not in "()!&|"))
    for cls in filter_unary:
        f = pp.Literal(f"~{cls.code}") + unary_end
```
- **Why:** with only `)` excluded, `(~s &~q)` parsed but `(~s&~q)` didn't. That's the same bug with a different character after the name, and `~c 200&~q` already parsed. A maintainer would reasonably ask why the fix stops at one character. `( ) ! & |` are exactly the characters the grammar uses as brackets and operators.
- **Still rejected:** characters that aren't operators, like `~sx`, `~allx`, `~s.`, `~s-x`, `~s~q` and quotes. So a mistyped name still raises an error instead of quietly turning into something like an AND with a URL match.
- **Smaller points:** the character set is built once outside the loop, and the comment explains why this `WordEnd` isn't the default.

**2. Tests: placed next to the tests they relate to**
- `test_nesting_unary` now also checks the nested case `((~s) & (~q | ~e))`, including the tree shape.
- `test_binaryops` checks that `~s&~q` parses as an AND, `~s|~q` as an OR, and `~s!~q` as `~s` ANDed with a NOT.
- `test_parse_err` now also checks that `~s.` is rejected. `~s.` stood for the characters that must keep failing, so the wider fix can't accidentally accept them.

**3. Changelog wording** now says "a closing parenthesis or an operator, e.g. `!(~s)` or `~s&~q`", because the fix covers more than brackets.

## Edge cases I checked and didn't need to change
- **Nested brackets:** `((~s))`, `!(!(~s))`, `((~s) & (~q))` and `(~s & (~q | ~e))` all parse correctly.
- **Leading and trailing whitespace**, including tabs and newlines inside brackets: already worked before the fix, and still does.
- **Unbalanced input:** `~s(`, `~a)`, `~all)` and `~u foo)` are still rejected, as they should be.
- **One behaviour to know about:** `~s(~q)` now parses as `~s & ~q`. That matches how `~s (~q)` already behaved, but if you'd rather keep rejecting it, take `(` out of the excluded set.

## Left alone on purpose
- **`~h foo&~q` parses its argument as the regex `foo&`.** This is existing behaviour for filters that take a regex. "Fixing" it would change what valid regexes mean, since `|` is a legitimate regex character, so it's out of scope.
- **The existing `test_binaryops` has two bare `isinstance(...)` calls with no `assert`**, so those lines check nothing. My new lines use `assert`. I didn't rewrite the old ones because they aren't part of this change, but they'd be a reasonable one-line follow-up.

I reproduced the bug: with `hardump=~/out.har`, mitmdump reads every flow and then fails on exit, and no HAR file is written.

**What I ran**, with HOME set to a fresh temporary directory, `/tmp/hardump_home.IydBRA`:
```

```

```
     << HTTP/2.0 200 OK 1.2k
127.0.0.1:51727: POST https://httpbin.org/post HTTP/2.0
     << HTTP/2.0 200 OK 453b
[05:27:23.659] Addon error: [Errno 2] No such file or directory: '~/out.har'
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File ".../mitmproxy/addons/savehar.py", line 128, in done
    self.export_har(self.flows, ctx.options.hardump)
  File ".../mitmproxy/command.py", line 322, in wrapper
    return function(*args, **kwargs)
  File ".../mitmproxy/addons/savehar.py", line 44, in export_har
    with open(path, "wb") as f:
FileNotFoundError: [Errno 2] No such file or directory: '~/out.har'
exit=0
```
- Both flows were read and kept in memory, then the write failed when `done` ran.
- Afterwards the temporary HOME held only the `.mitmproxy/` CA files mitmproxy creates on startup. There was no `out.har` there, and no literal `./~` directory in the repo.
- **The process still exits 0.** The error is logged as an addon error and doesn't fail the run, so a script wrapping mitmdump wouldn't notice the HAR is missing.

**The `save.har` command does handle `~`.** I confirmed this with `/tmp/hardump_repro/save_har_cmd.py`, using the same HOME:
```
save.har path argument: ~/cmd.har -> /tmp/hardump_home.IydBRA/cmd.har
cmd.har written to HOME: True
```

**Why the two paths differ.** The expansion happens in the command layer, not in `export_har` itself:
- `export_har` declares `path: types.Path` (`savehar.py:36`).
- When a command is run from the UI or command line, its arguments go through `command.parsearg`. For a `Path` argument that calls `_PathType.parse`, which is `return os.path.expanduser(s)` (`types.py:210-211`).
- `done()` calls `self.export_har(self.flows, ctx.options.hardump)` directly from Python (`savehar.py:128`). The `@command.command` wrapper only checks argument types and then calls the function (`command.py:320-322`), so nothing expands `~`. The raw string `~/out.har` reaches `open()` on line 44.
- `hardump` is declared as a plain `str` option (`savehar.py:79-88`). Nothing expands it when it's set either.

Other path options in the codebase expand `~` where they're used: `save.py:30` (`save_stream_file`), `readfile.py:62` and `tlsconfig.py:350`. The natural fix is to do the same for `hardump` in `done()`, for example `os.path.expanduser(ctx.options.hardump)`, and leave the `"-"` (stdout) case alone. I haven't changed anything for this bug yet; you only asked for the reproduction.

steps.text:
## Root cause

The value of the `hardump` option goes straight to `open()` and is never passed through `os.path.expanduser`. Expansion only happens when a path is typed as a command argument. `hardump` is read as an option, so it never gets that treatment.

**1. `hardump` is a plain string option** (`mitmproxy/addons/savehar.py:79-88`):
```python
        loader.add_option(
            "hardump",
            str,
            "",
            ...
```
The option system stores `~/out.har` exactly as typed. Declaring it as `str` doesn't mark it as a path, so nothing expands it.

**2. On exit, `done()` passes that raw string to `export_har`** (`savehar.py:122-128`):
```python
    def done(self):
        if ctx.options.hardump:
            if ctx.options.hardump == "-":
                ...
            else:
                self.export_har(self.flows, ctx.options.hardump)
```

**3. `export_har` opens whatever path it's given** (`savehar.py:35-36`, `:44`):
```python
    @command.command("save.har")
    def export_har(self, flows: Sequence[flow.Flow], path: types.Path) -> None:
        ...
        with open(path, "wb") as f:
```
`open("~/out.har")` treats `~` as an ordinary directory name, so it raises `FileNotFoundError`.

**Why `save.har` works and `hardump` doesn't.** The `path: types.Path` annotation only has an effect when the function is run as a command. Typed commands get their string arguments converted by `command.parsearg` (`command.py:312`, `return t.parse(manager, argtype, spec)`). For `Path` that calls this (`mitmproxy/types.py:210-211`):
```python
    def parse(self, manager: "CommandManager", t: type, s: str) -> str:
        return os.path.expanduser(s)
```
`done()` calls the Python method directly, and the decorator's wrapper only checks argument types before calling the function (`command.py:320-322`):
```python
        def wrapper(*args, **kwargs):
            verify_arg_signature(function, args, kwargs)
            return function(*args, **kwargs)
```
So `export_har` expects its caller to have expanded the path already. Commands do that for it. `done()` doesn't.

**Why it fails at the end, after the whole session.** `configure` never checks the path (`savehar.py:100-102`):
```python
        if "hardump" in updated:
            if not ctx.options.hardump:
                self.flows = []
```
The path is first used in `done()`. By then every flow has been collected in `self.flows` (`:116-120`), so the error loses all of them. The exception is logged as an addon error and the process still exits 0. That makes two separate problems:
- **The bug:** `~` is never expanded.
- **What makes it costly:** the path isn't validated until shutdown, and the failure doesn't change the exit code.

## How the other file options handle a leading `~`

Each of these addons calls `expanduser` on its option value in its own code before opening the file. None relies on the command layer.

**`save_stream_file`**: the `_path` helper in `mitmproxy/addons/save.py:25-30`:
```python
@lru_cache
def _path(path: str) -> str:
    """Extract the path from a path spec (which may have an extra "+" at the front)"""
    if path.startswith("+"):
        path = path[1:]
    return os.path.expanduser(path)
```
Both the option path (`save.py:89`, `path = datetime.today().strftime(_path(ctx.options.save_stream_file))`) and the `save.file` command (`:139`) use this helper. The command's argument has already been expanded, and running `expanduser` twice does no harm. The option is also checked as soon as it's set: `configure` opens the file right away (`:77-82`) and turns any `OSError` into an `OptionsError`. A bad `save_stream_file` path therefore fails at startup, not on exit.

**`rfile`**: `mitmproxy/addons/readfile.py:61-64`:
```python
    async def load_flows_from_path(self, path: str) -> int:
        path = os.path.expanduser(path)
        try:
            with open(path, "rb") as f:
```
The option is declared as `Optional[str]` (`:28`), and `running()` passes it as-is to `doread` (`:77-79`). The expansion is in this function.

**`server_replay`**: expanded in the shared helper `mitmproxy/io/io.py:97-111`:
```python
def read_flows_from_paths(paths) -> list[flow.Flow]:
    ...
        for path in paths:
            path = os.path.expanduser(path)
            with open(path, "rb") as f:
```
The option is declared as `Sequence[str]` (`serverplayback.py:88-92`). `configure` calls the helper immediately (`:260-265`) and turns read errors into `OptionsError`, so this option is also checked at startup. The `replay.server.file` command goes through the same helper (`:158-160`).

## Checked by running each option

I used a fresh temporary HOME, `/tmp/tilde_home.dWvsYX`, with a copy of `successful_log.mitm` saved there as `in.mitm`:

| Option | Value | Result |
|---|---|---|
| `rfile` | `~/in.mitm` | read the flows, exit 0 |
| `save_stream_file` | `~/stream.mitm` | wrote `$HOME/stream.mitm` (17,394 bytes) |
| `server_replay` | `~/in.mitm` | loaded 2 flows |
| `server_replay` | `~/missing.mitm` | `OptionsError: No such file or directory`, raised from `configure` |
| **`hardump`** | **`~/out.har`** | **`FileNotFoundError: ... '~/out.har'` on exit, no file written** |

Afterwards the temporary HOME contained only `in.mitm` and `stream.mitm`.

My first `server_replay` run never finished. Once replay flows are loaded, mitmdump keeps serving and waits for clients. I stopped it and checked that option in-process through the addon's `configure` hook instead.

## What this means for a fix

To match the other options, `done()` should expand the path before writing, for example `os.path.expanduser(ctx.options.hardump)`, leaving the `"-"` stdout case unchanged. A follow-up could also make `configure` reject a path whose directory doesn't exist, as `save_stream_file` and `server_replay` already do at startup. That way a bad path wouldn't cost a whole session's flows. That second change is more than the reported bug, so it's your call whether to include it. ## What I changed

**The `hardump` changelog entry.** It said the bug "made mitmdump fail on exit". `SaveHar` is in `default_addons()` (`mitmproxy/addons/__init__.py:63`), so `hardump` behaves the same way in mitmproxy, mitmweb and mitmdump, and naming only mitmdump would mislead anyone scanning release notes for the other tools. It now reads:
```markdown
- Fix the `hardump` option not expanding a leading `~` in its path, which made writing the HAR file
  fail on exit with `FileNotFoundError` and lose the collected flows.
```

## Edge cases I checked that didn't need changes

I ran each `hardump` case through the addon with a temporary HOME and a temporary working directory. The script is `/tmp/hardump_review/edges.py`.

- **Windows `USERPROFILE`.** I can't run Windows here, so I called `ntpath.expanduser` directly, which applies Windows' rules on any OS:
  - Windows ignores `HOME` (since Python 3.8). It uses `USERPROFILE`, then falls back to `HOMEDRIVE`+`HOMEPATH`.
  - The new test sets both `HOME` and `USERPROFILE`, like `test_types.py:86-87`, so it should pass on Windows CI too.
  - `~/out.har` expands to `C:\Users\t/out.har` there. Windows accepts mixed separators, and `~\out.har` works as well.
- **Empty `hardump`.** Nothing is written and nothing fails. `done()` returns early (`if ctx.options.hardump:`), so an empty value never reaches `export_har`.
- **`-` (stdout).** Unaffected: it's handled before `export_har` is called, and I checked it end to end earlier.
- **Relative path.** `rel.har` is written to the current directory, as before. `expanduser` leaves it untouched.
- **`~` not at the start.** `a~b.har` is written literally, because only a leading `~` is expanded.
- **`~/c.zhar`.** Still compressed. The `.zhar` check runs on the unexpanded path, which still ends in `.zhar`.
- **Error messages are clearer now.** `~/missing/x.har` fails with the expanded absolute path in the message, not `'~/missing/x.har'`.

## Other things I considered and left alone

- **A missing parent directory** (`sub/rel.har`, `~/missing/x.har`) still fails at exit. `save_stream_file` creates missing directories and validates its path in `configure`, so it fails at startup. That's the follow-up I mentioned earlier, and it's a behaviour change beyond this bug.

Neither fix needs a documentation change, so I haven't edited anything under `docs/`.

## Filter expressions: no change

Filter syntax is documented in one place, `docs/src/content/concepts/filters.md`, which has two parts:
- **The filter table**, built from code by `docs/scripts/filters.py`. It lists each filter's code and the help text from `flowfilter.help`. My fix doesn't touch either, so the table comes out the same.
- **Hand-written notes and examples** (lines 15-21 and 44-58). None of them tells users to put a space after a filter like `~s` before a `)` or an operator, so nothing describes the old behaviour. The documented example `!(~q & ~t "text/html")` already shows brackets around filters; it only worked before because `~t` takes an argument.

I parsed every filter example in the docs with the fix in place, and all of them still give the same result:
- the five examples in `filters.md`: `google\.com`, `~q ~b test`, `!(~q & ~t "text/html")`, `~u "get(Info|Routers)"` and the `~u <regex>` tutorial example
- `~m post` from `_index.md:89`

I considered adding an example like `!(~s)`, but the docs never claimed it fails, and the CHANGELOG entry already covers the fix.

## `hardump`: no change

There is no hand-written page for `hardump`. A search under `docs/` finds no mention of it, of HAR files or of `save_stream_file`. All options are documented in a table that `docs/scripts/options.py` builds from each option's help text. For `hardump` that text is in `savehar.py:84-87`:

> Save a HAR file with all flows on exit. You may select particular flows by setting save_stream_filter. For mitmdump, enabling this option will mean that flows are kept in memory.

It says nothing about `~`, and neither do the help texts of the options that already expanded `~`:
- `save_stream_file` (`save.py:55-58`)
- `rfile` ("Read flows from file.", `readfile.py:28`)
- `server_replay` ("Replay server responses from a saved file.", `serverplayback.py:92`)

So the docs never promised `~` expansion for any file option. The fix makes `hardump` behave like the others, which is what the docs already imply. Adding "supports `~`" to `hardump` alone would make it the only file option that mentions it.

So the changes are still the two code fixes, their tests, and the two CHANGELOG entries. Nothing is committed.
